blocks.x: I'm John Fuhannes. I'm from Minneapolis, University of Minnesota.
And we're here at the New Orleans Hotel, talking to Armin Hug, pianist from New Orleans. Is that your real name? And Dick Allen of the New Orleans Archives. Armin, is that your real name, Armin Hug?
Yes, that's from my real name. Armin Hug, that's right. And you didn't ask me where I was born at.
No, I never have known your full name.
Armin, my full name?
Yeah.
Oh, Dick, please. Don't tell me. Armin, Oscar Hug. Okay.
You know, I never have known the Oscar.
Yeah, well, that's neat, isn't it?
Yeah.
To use a modern expression. Yeah.
Okay. Yeah. And my name's Dick Allen. That's what I've got to say. I didn't know.
And my good friend, Mr. Henry Fuhidu, just passed through.

Okay. You can tell us all about him. He can tell us all about Bump John or something. Okay. Well, take over, John. I'll move the microphones back. I didn't want to interrupt. Just open up to the track.
You were born here at Armin in New Orleans. And you stayed here most of your life. You haven't gone out anymore.

That's right, John. I was born on Tulane Avenue. Dick is the one that told me this because I could never find out what street I was actually born on. But he knew it was somewhere on Tulane Avenue. And finally, my present wife was looking at some of the old photographs of my mother and father. And on the back of them, very, very faint now. You can't make it out very well. But you can see 2507 Tulane that these photographs were probably penciled at that time. And I imagine that was the address, 2507 Tulane Avenue.
I see.

And I've been here all my life. I've never been anywhere. I have been maybe 100 miles or so out of the city. But never to stay, you know, maybe on a short trip for a day or so or something like that. But I've never really been out of New Orleans.
Do you have a particular reason? Is there a major reason why you never left New Orleans?

Well, a major reason, I guess you could say is that basically I was just a sort of a, maybe you might say a country boy at heart. But even though I was born in New Orleans, I like the simplicity of the city at that time. Of course, it's changed a lot now over the past years. But at that time, I like the simplicity of it. The nostalgic things, the friendliness, the, I don't know, just that you seem to know everyone. Everywhere you went, you know somebody. And music just seemed to be destined for me. I use that word destined because I believe to a certain degree that this is what it must have been. Because everywhere I went, I heard music. You know, you hear the sounds on the river, the street parades, the funerals. Even in those days, they had the old German bands before the First World War. They used to go around on the street corners and play for pennies and nickels, whatever you'd give them, you know.
Did they come right down Tulane Avenue?

Not on Tulane. They used to, well, they may have had, yeah, they had parades, I suppose, on Tulane Avenue. But, of course, I remember later on when we moved to Taunty Street, which was a little ways about two or three blocks off of Tulane Avenue. But I stayed in that vicinity pretty much. And, of course, as I say, you couldn't help but grow up with the sounds of music around you. Because everywhere there was something going on all the time. Parties. Right, Dick?
Yeah.
Walk down the street, you hear a piano playing somewhere.
Is that why you decided to take the piano? Or was it any conscious thought you were on?

I had no reason, John. John, I had no other reason but that I just loved this sound and I wanted to do it. I don't know. I can't say that I wanted to do it to prove anything. I just wanted to play it. And my mother had a piano. She had one of these old upright pianos.
Right in your house.

Right in your house. Yeah, right in the house. And she played a little bit. Not very well. She would have loved to play. But she played a very bad bass. She played a good treble. But the bass, oh, she used the same bass for every key, you know. But Lord, she really gave me a good start and she showed me the notes, you know. And it really gave me, I guess, the incentive that I needed.
I see. Did she play any particular kind of piano or just a...

No, she could just play the waltzes and read a little bit, you know. And she played a little... She could just stumble through things to a grade. She only took about three or four months of lessons, you know.
Did you have a formal teacher that taught you?

Well, I started off, like I say, with my mother. And, of course, my uncle, Dui Shmead, who was known as Wilbur Leroy, and show business, he was a vaudeville, I can't. He played a little fake piano, you know. And he used to always encourage me, you know, and show me little tricks and chords and things that he used to know. And, of course, I know that all of this was a great incentive for me, but somehow or another, I don't know how to explain this, but I just didn't know anything else. It's the only thing I knew. I had no desire to become a doctor, a lawyer, an architect, an engineer, not even to be a millionaire. I wasn't even thinking of money. Like today, everybody thinks of how much they're going to make, you know. I mean, when I was playing, I wasn't thinking of how much I was going to make, or whether I was going to be able to make enough to retire the first five years I was playing or the first ten years. All I wanted to do was to play that piano and say I could play it. Not to say, not to have the satisfaction of saying I could play it, but because I really wanted to play it. This is the one thing I want to do. And I never missed an opportunity to pick up anything that I've heard. Of course, you never had the advantages that you have today. You know, I mean, radio was at a minimum, and you had very little records that you could listen to, and no sound equipment or anything. But, of course, you had the old player pianos, you know, that you could listen to.
Now, was ragtime the popular style piano then? Would you say that?

Well, I would say to a great extent they were playing things around here that sounded like ragtime. Yeah, I guess there were many piano players, and as a matter of fact, I know Dick can discuss this a lot better than I can because he's gone into this and researched it, all that sort of thing. My feelings, my feelings is that ragtime is basically not in the wall of music. Is that right now? I mean, although it might have been played here, we might have played it.
Yeah, it seems to me that it came here from another place. I think, didn't it? And there was some ragtime performances here, but I'd have shut the door. Thank the Lord.
Well, I'm glad we're getting some privacy now.
Yeah. Well, anyway.
Well, yeah, tell us a little bit about that. No, no. You know a little bit more about that than I do. Maybe I may be wrong in saying that, how did I play that?
Well, I think they played...
I think they played ragtime.
They played it here, but they played a lot of other things, and you remember what they played.

I think, John, that I would say that ragtime was something that was a syncopated kind of music that was started, where it started at, I couldn't truthfully say. They say that a lot of people say it started up in St. Louis, a lot of people say it started in various other parts, but I don't know. I couldn't say that. But I guess probably that, as Dick says, it drifted... If it did start somewhere else, naturally, it would be only natural that the musicians here would have picked up on it to a certain extent. But I might add this, John, that to my knowledge, the musicians here that played music when I came were not playing just ragtime. They were playing a lot of other things besides ragtime. And I would say that this makes... This is where the difference came in. That in New Orleans, I think you could go and walk down the street, you'd hear some piano player in a saloon playing blues on some old beat-up piano. But it was a real great sound, you know, just a slow blues. You couldn't put your finger on it. You couldn't tell what it was. I couldn't tell you right now what they were playing, but you could tell it was something real good. And that's what I think is making New Orleans.
Did you ever get up to the Storyville area? And supposedly the pianos were playing in the Storyville area.
Well, I could say this, that I can remember walking around in that area, but of course you must remember that it closed 1918. That's correct. According to what we know or what we read about.
Well, that's what they read, but that's not what Luke's hero says, and he used to sell ice cream there.
It was still going. So he ought to know. It was still going on that, wasn't it?
It was still going.
It was still going.
It was still going.

Why, sure. That's what I told somebody the other night. I said, you know, I said, you know, officially it may have closed down. I said, but don't kid yourself that there wasn't a lot of it still in existence. Even when I was about maybe, say, 12 or 13 years old, when I used to go around walking around on Basin Street, I can remember Eddie Miller and I and Shockey and Julian Lane, or I could have mentioned many musicians that we used to go around there, and we used to encounter lots of the girls, you know, like they're doing today, the same thing. They were in their little cubby holes, you know, and they were operating, I'm sure. And there was still the sounds of a little piano playing here and there, you know, so I'm sure that it was still going on, even though officially it had closed down.
Well, most people don't realize that a lot of it was there. You know, where charity is now.
That's out of the street.
Right. Yeah, there were a lot of girls in there. Right. Now, Foujira, never mind, I won't put that on there. Well, Foujira says it's a lot cheaper there. Or the other world said that.
It was a lot cheaper there.
Would you say that your, the important influences, the piano style, the piano playing that influenced you came from that area more than any other? From the parades?

John, this is something now, you asked me a very good question. I like that question because that's very good. I can say that even though my basic love was piano, no. These piano players, even though they were beautiful, it was not the only thing that influenced me. Just a drum beat coming down the street was a great inspiration. Just to hear that beat. I see. Or just to hear a two or three or four piece band playing somewhere. Or to hear a bunch of guys get together that could hardly play. But at least they had the feeling, the spirit, you know. I mean, all of these things, I mean, they had a great influence on me.
And most piano players, I take it around that time, let's say, set in 1915 or 1910 or whatever. You were born in 1910. We're band pianists.

They weren't so pianists. Band pianists, right. And you see, a lot of the good pianists that had kind of left around here by the time that I was coming up. Jelly Roll had been, Jelly Roll was gone. Clarence Williams was gone. Clarence Williams was gone. Clarence Williams was gone. Tony Jackson was gone. You had many, many, I guess, were still around here. You had many local fellows, local pianists around town. Steve Lewis was around here, which was an excellent, excellent black pianist. Wonderful. And, well, like I say, the pianist, I always, I always loved the pianist. You know, anywhere there was a piano player, that was, that was my, my, my ideal right there. But really, I got inspiration from, from many of the marching bands. Just listening to, listening to them play, play that feudal music, and, and, and happy marching music, you know. The marching music, I think, is so inspirational. If this doesn't inspire you, well, you just don't have music in you, that's all. It inspires you to do greater things, let me put it that way. It inspired me.
Did they, did the marching bands play Dixieland? Was that a term?
They always played two beat, don't you think, Chad?
Oh yeah, I'm sure.

We say, we, we use the term two beat, but, well, not two beat, uh, just, March music, which was traditional. New Orleans March music. New Orleans March music, which is, Monk, Monk Hazel used to always tell me, he used to always say, oh man, I hate to, hate to hear him use the word Dixieland,
Yeah.

and, and type you with, with just Dixieland, because he says, really, it's New Orleans music, you know. Of course, Dixieland, we know it's, it's part of this, part of this scene too. But actually, it's New Orleans music. Yeah. Right. And of course, uh, as, as you said, you know, asked me, how did I get this inspiration? Or what did it inspire me to? stuff

it does inspire you to great things. Of course, it inspired me to really something real great, which is a question that I think you will be leading up to later on, but I'm not going to approach this until you get into it.

I remember you mentioned in another interview once, Armand, that you started to play piano at a time when the Dixieland and Ragtime styles were crossing or something like that. And could you just elaborate on that a little bit?

Well, yes. I would say that they were crossing. Of course, I was not aware of what was happening because to me it was music, as I said before. New Orleans was just New Orleans to me. I knew nothing else, and I only knew the musicians in New Orleans here, the ones I was associated with, and what they played and what they stood for. And I mean, this is the only thing that I knew. Now, as far as the styles crossing, yes, I would probably say that maybe the Dixieland and Ragtime was crossing because in 1917, 1918, the original Dixieland jazz band had already made its big hit in New York.
Right.

And I'm sure that Dixieland was then becoming the craze going into the 20s, you know, into the early 20s. And surely the music was going through a lot of changes right around that time. As far as the Ragtime, the pure Ragtime, I'm sure that the pure Ragtime was beginning to fall back of what was happening because up until that time maybe all they knew was, you know, what Ragtime was. But then when they began realizing the difference between the New Orleans music and the beat and the style and the way the New Orleans musicians played, it made a big difference. That was, as you say, that was probably where it was starting to cross, you know, right there.
And I understand the word jazz was not used then, that Ragtime was the word.
Well, as Dick knows, he, once again, I say this goes back into a technical part of the history of jazz, which has always been very...
Because what I know, I've talked to the older musicians and taped their stories, and they would remember things from when Almond was, before Almond was born.
Right.
You know, we've got guys like Jack Lane who was born in 1873.
Papa Lane. Right.
And he remembered way back there. Long. Well, I guess when you were born, he would...
Gee, when I was born...
He was almost ready to retire for music.
He was about ready to retire. I would say so.
Can I ask a silly question?
Yeah.

Maybe, but, you know, it isn't just the music that interests me. It's also the people and the way the people like music and, you know, what music did for them. And I was thinking once, somebody like Sal Gutierrez, one of those people from up around Coliseum Square showed me a picture once. I think you were playing baseball. Would it have been?
Probably so. Yeah. I did.
Different people from the neighborhood. Baseball.
We used to play ball out on Coliseum Square there.
Yeah.
Yeah. Now. That's right.
At ball games, did you ever hear a band?
A band? Oh, yeah. They had bands. But I can't tell you who it was.
Yeah. I mean, it just was something there.
They always had music. Yeah.
Everywhere you went. How did it work?

The prize fights, when they used to have fights, you know, they used to have a wagon or a truck, and they had bands playing, advertising the fights, and some good bands. So it was always good music. But you see, people, always in New Orleans here, people just took things for granted. I mean, you know, they didn't think that this was ever going to be something historic. At the time that they were playing in wagons and trucks advertising the prize fights, you don't think that they ever thought that this would be part of a New Orleans jazz figure, you know. I mean, it was just the regular thing that was happening here, that's all.
Well, your uncle was in the circus?
My uncle was in vaudeville. No, he wasn't in circus. He was a vaudeville comedian. He was a straight man, and he had a black-faced comedian that used to do the comedy work with him, you know.
I see.
And he did give me a lot of encouragement.
When you started playing in your early jobs, did you solo piano, or did you play as a member of the band?

When I first started, John, I would say that I played more so with little combinations. Like, for instance, you know, little groups, maybe three or four pieces. My first job, first professional job was in silent movie houses. That was with a three-piece group, drum, violin, and piano. And we played at the neighborhood shows, you know.
While the film was going?

Yeah, silent films, you know. We'd play music that was supposed to be appropriate. Half the time we didn't know what we were playing for, you know, but we'd be playing something. I can remember seeing Rudolph Valentino pictures, you know, and the Keystone Cops, you know, the Max Sonnet comedies and all that sort of thing. I used to play for all of that stuff, but with a little group. I didn't play by myself. It was a little combination.
I see. And violin, of course, was a very important instrument, I think, earlier in jazz.

Violin fit in pretty good, yeah. I believe it or not, that fellow that played there with me, his name was Neil Grasshofer. I haven't seen that fellow since I played, and that was in 19, about 1923, 24. And I haven't seen him since.
Maybe he's changed.
Then, from there, you went to...

Well, my most important job after that, John, was in the Fern Dance Hall. And where was that? That was on Iberville, or as Dick says, Ziverville, on Iberville Street. And it was one of the leading dance halls in the city, always was, you know, and they had good jazz bands there. And I got the opportunity to play there. Of course, this was the big thing for me. I was about 14, just ready to turn 15, you know. And, I mean, this was a great big thing for me.
Can you just mention a few of the names?

Oh, yes. I remember, for sure, they had... Broken Dishes. Von Gammon. Oh, well, he's talking about my girlfriend now. Broken... I'm just kidding. She could have been. Broken Dishes, who really used to be a real tough girl. She used to beat up all the other girls, you know. She was tattooed. She was tattooed from head to foot. You know, the girls were working on tickets, you know. They'd try to beat one another out of dances, and she'd go back in, and she'd have it out with them. But it was all really part of the scene, I guess. It only added interest to it. But anyhow, you asked me about the band. The drummer was Von Gammon at the time I went there. He was the leader. Very nice person. And Harry Shields. Larry Shields' brother was playing clarinet. And a fellow by the name of Buzzy Willards playing banjo. A fellow by the name of Bill Gillen playing trumpet. Oh, incidentally, I might mention here, sounded a lot like Biggs.
Bill Gillen?

Oh, Bill Gillen, he played a lot. What year was that? This was in 1920, about 1926, about 25, 26. And Bill Gillen was singing the blues solo, you know, that Biggs had made. And he got to, you know, people used to, all the musicians used to kid him about it. They used to call him Biggs. You know, they said, call him Biggs, play that solo for us, you know. And he did a great job on it. But somehow or another, he never followed music as a career.
Is he still around?

I really don't know. I haven't seen him. God, I guess I haven't seen him in years. I know he, I never heard of him playing anywhere or playing any jobs. After I left the foreign, I never played with him again. That was the last time. But he played very well. And the bass, I don't think we had a bass.
So, that was it. Well, he, did he listen to Biggs records? Oh, yeah. I mean, he knew them.
Oh, he was a great admirer. Yes, he was a great admirer of Biggs. So, you see, Biggs was already making a big imprint on the people, the musicians down here.
And then you went and played in the French Quarter for a while, I guess.

I went to work at a cabaret. It was called the Cabarets in those days. It was called the Valencia Cabaret. It was where the Royal Sinesta Hotel is today, on Bourbon Street. And I worked with various little groups, three-piece groups there, from time to time. Some of the musicians I played with there was Chink Morton's son, Chink Morton Jr. Eddie Miller played there with me for a while. Who's now playing with Pete Fountain. Yes. And Eddie played alto sax in those days. He wasn't playing tenor. And Al Hesman, banjo player. I'll never forget the night that Leonor Pola, a famous Rhythm Kings clarinet player, came in town. He was hospitalized, you know, for many years.
Yes.

And he was out on pass or something. And he stopped in. And I have just a very, very faint recollection of him sitting in with me, you know, and playing. But, of course, this was a very great thrill for me to know just the fact. I remember that I know he sat in. And I couldn't tell you too much about his playing because, as I say, it was a long time ago, you know. But I do know that he came in there and sat down with us and played a couple of sets, you know.
Was Sharky, did you also play with Sharky?
Oh, I played with Sharky many times. Yes, many, many, many times.
Of course, he went to, he took Bix's place in the Wolverines.
They sent him to take Bix's place when Bix left the Wolverines. That's right.
I'm not sure he stayed too long.

No, he didn't stay too long because the truth of the matter is, is that it was a very hard thing for Sharky to take, I'm sure, because it did not prove successful for Sharky to go there and take Bix's place. You know, that was a tough job to ask anybody to do, any trumpet player to go and take Bix's place at that particular time.
Well, how could he fit the style of that band?
That's just it.
It wasn't his style.

And it wasn't his style. And you know, this, I think, really did something to Sharky because he never would say very much if you mentioned Bix around him. And I can understand it, you know, I mean, it kind of gave him a terrible complex, I guess. But really, he wasn't deserving of this because it was a mistake. I think it was Paul Merez or someone who thought that Sharky could fill that bill, you see. Oh, I see. But Sharky's style, as Dick Allen says, anyone who knew Sharky would just know that Sharky was not the top trumpet player to play the style that Bix was playing.
What, as close as you can figure out, what was the style of that Wolverines group? Was it, did they connect it all with any more?
The Wolverines, as I once spoke to a fellow around here that used to play saxophone. I don't know if you ever did get to meet him, Cy Gerard.
Never did. You told me about him, I never met him.
Wonderful character. It's too bad that you missed him.
Yeah, we wanted to get together.

He was the most, he was a very, very, very charming, interesting person. He was one of these fellows, I never did know too much about his saxophone player, but he knew everything. You could ask him something about what was happening, you know, and one of these kind of fellows, he could tell you everything that was happening and always knew everything. And he knew everything about the New Orleans Rhythm Kings and everything that happened. And once I was talking to him and he told me something that I had in my mind and he told me the same thing and it coincided exactly what I had in mind. He says, don't you think, Oman, he says that the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, or rather, how did he put that now? The New Orleans Rhythm Kings was an improvement on the original Dixieland Jazz Band.
Yeah.
And he says, don't you think that the Wolverines was an improvement on the New Orleans Rhythm Kings? Of course, that's kind of putting it kind of strong.
Yeah.

And I am from New Orleans, and I hate to say this, but I do think that in some respects that maybe the Rhythm Kings was some kind of an improvement in many ways. As far as harmonies and new ideas, you know, for little introductions and endings and things that the Rhythm Kings were playing very simple things. They were playing things that was real, basic New Orleans music, which is nothing wrong, which I dearly love. But, of course, we must admit that Bix came along and did change things to a degree, because, after all, his solos were so inventive.
Yes.
And right now I realize that I'm getting into talking about Bix, which you haven't really asked me too much about yet.

Well, we're getting up to it, and I think one of the things that we're getting to is how the New Orleans musicians influenced him. And what we owe to the New Orleans musicians, or New Orleans for, you know, there's a big controversy about this.
Well.
And some say he departed very radically from it.

Well, I think that this is a very good thing to think about. That's why I have no misgivings about saying that the Wolverines was an improvement on the New Orleans Rhythm Kings. But I'm only meaning that from, you know, constructive criticism, because I do think that Bix basically worshipped New Orleans musicians deep in his heart, even though he was far advanced in his theory. He basically...

followed that style. In other words, you can listen to his records and see that the pattern of the Dixieland music and the Rhythm Kings and the Walden's music was there, excepting that he used his own ideas, his solos and his phrasing and things like that, which you couldn't say that that was anything wrong, excepting that it was a great new sound.
Well, Herman, where shall we place Emmett Hardy in relation to Bix?

Emmett Hardy, John, that's something I have heard of. I've often wondered about it. How can you tell? What can you say? I didn't know him. No one had a recording of him, did they? I don't think so, did they? I never found him. They said, Monk Hazel said there was a cylinder disc that was made of him, but no one has ever really found it. And Monk Hazel, who I dearly loved as a friend and as a musician, I think Monk really, really knew what he was talking about when he told you something. And Monk said that he thought that Emmett sounded a lot like Bix. He always said that. He used to always tell me that. And of course, a lot of people said, well, I just don't believe that anybody sounded like Bix. You know, in other words, it could have been possible. That someone would have sounded like Bix before Bix, let's put it that way. Before Bix. And this was Monk's contention that somewhere along the line, Bix had heard Emmett Hardy. Now, whether or not this is so, I could say. But it's a thought and it's something to think about. Because once again, it would be a great thing if we had known for certain that Emmett Hardy had really had any influence on Bix. Because somewhere along the line, someone has always had an influence on someone. Right, Bill?
Oh, yeah.
We know definitely that King Oliver influenced Louis. And others before King Oliver influenced him. It went on down the line, you see. But who did influence Bix with that sound?

Well, I guess a lot of musicians who have played with Hardy, I guess Ray Burt was one that played with him early. But I forgot what interview it was. They were talking about his sound being the pure New Orleans sound, but with a sweet tone that was not characteristic of New Orleans sound. But they say that Buddy Molden, too. But also that Emmett had played in Davenport for a while, and Bix had heard him there. And that he...
I got the second reel on. Okay. Mr. Huck. Ready to go. Okay. You want to ask a question?

Yeah, well, it's just that is there any value in trying to say that... trying to trace this to Emmett Hardy or what? I mean, it's obvious that Emmett Hardy was probably a great musician. I mean, you know, a lot of people testify to that. And that he probably had an influence on Bix's style. But what did Bix have... what did he contribute to the course of musical development? I guess you could say of jazz since the New Orleans style. Was his influence or contribution musically a harmonic in his use of harmonies? Or... Then I'm going to ask you to play some piano in which you kind of point out what he did, what he seems to have contributed. Yeah, you mean what Bix contributed?

Right. Well, I can only say that as far as I'm concerned, he contributed. He contributed so much that it would be just hard to say what he did contribute, accepting that we know that all of these solos that he played were so original and so meaningful and so beautiful that really, if you analyze each one of his solos, they become almost... They become a masterpiece. Each one of them are a masterpiece. And you can almost make a tune or an arrangement out of each one of his solos. Yeah. Which is so amazing. I mean, you hardly hear anyone who had such original solos as he had. The only ones that come to my mind is like Armstrong and Bonnie Berrigan. You know, a few people that really had solos that really stayed with you. I mean, so that you couldn't forget them. How long since you've heard a Bix record? How long since you've heard one? Well, I haven't played one now. Quite about six months a year, maybe.
Yeah, and you remember every solo. Pretty near. Very few of them. That's the most fantastic thing. And he remembers Trumbau by solos, too.

Trumbau. Frankie Trumbau, to me, I think that he was really great. I mean, to me, he is very, very underrated. Uh-huh. Even to when he was playing with Bix, Bix was so strong, you see, that he overshadowed anyone and everyone. And, of course, I think that really Trumbau did a lot to enhance him when they were playing together. Uh-huh. Because it seemed as though that Trumbau knew every move that he made. Uh-huh. There was nothing that Bix ever did that you wouldn't hear Trumbau right along with him. And it sounds as though you wouldn't know whether Trump, whether Bix got it from Trumbau or Trumbau got it from Bix. Uh-huh. I mean, you really couldn't figure it out. It was so close. Uh-huh. I think it was a beautiful team. Uh-huh. I don't know of any two musicians that complemented each other so well as they did. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Beautiful, beautiful combination. And I think they originated the so-called chase choruses in some of those numbers where back and forth they would answer each other.

Where they would answer one another. Yeah. Oh, definitely. That was beautiful. Yeah. You took advantage of me. And I can't start to think of all of the ones that they did that on. But it was just fantastic.
